the SEE sensitivity of the user circuit is dependent on its operating frequency, on the routing scheme, on the circuit complexity (number of logic gates and flip-flops) and that the SEE sensitivity is higher in the case of the user memory than in the case of configurable logic.

the SEE sensitivity of a circuit implemented in flash-based FPGA can be characterized by using heavy-ions radiation tests and that the sensitivity is strongly dependent on the operating frequency of the circuit.
the frequency dependence of SEE sensitivity in flash-based FPGAs depends on the routing scheme and the type of SEE.

the evaluation of the SEE sensitivity as a function of the working frequency and routing schemes.
the evaluation of SEE sensitivity in Flash-based FGPAs as a function of the working frequency and the routing scheme.
the characterization of the SEE sensitivity in Flash-based FPsGAs as a function of the operating frequency and different routing techniques.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
SEE sensitivity in Flash-based FGPAs is strongly frequency-dependent and can be reduced by using the routing scheme that minimizes the number of logic cells used to implement a circuit.
the SEE sensitivity is not constant as a function of the frequency.
the SEE sensitivity of Flash-based FPGA circuits is not a function of the frequency.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the frequency-dependent SEE sensitivity of a circuit is mainly determined by its combinational logic, while routing and sequential logic play a minor role.
the sensitivity of Flash-based FPGA circuits to SEEs is strongly related to the operating frequency and the routing scheme.
, as a rule of thumb, the frequency-dependent SEE sensitivity is mainly due to combinational logic, and the routing has a significant impact on the sensitivity of the circuit.
The main takeaway from our work is that

, while the frequency dependence is not negligible, it is possible to mitigate the SEE sensitivity with the proper routing of the circuit, thus allowing the use of Flash-based FPGas for space applications.
